Research

Research questions

The questions I am working on now, why, and what evidence would change my mind. The wider reading list is kept below as an archive.

Can interpretability become a cheap, standard part of model evaluation instead of a research project per model?

Why it matters to me: My position essay argues that explanation methods are rarely used in real evaluation because they are too costly and not meaningful enough. Probing and representation analysis on frozen models are the most promising candidates because they do not change the model being explained.

What would change my view: Evidence that frozen-model probes routinely disagree with causal interventions on the same model, or that they add nothing over held-out accuracy when choosing between models.

  • A research program for inspectable ML
  • Hewitt and Liang, Designing and Interpreting Probes with Control Tasks

Do machine-readable repository policies, enforced by deterministic checks, make coding agents more reliable than the same rules written in prose?

Why it matters to me: This is the question behind Beryl and my CP3106 independent research. Prose instructions are easy to write but give no evidence they were followed.

What would change my view: If agents given equivalent natural-language guidance pass as many hidden tests and policy checks as agents given enforced policies, the extra machinery is not earning its cost.

  • Beryl project page
  • Kapoor et al., AI Agents That Matter

Is learning usefully described as finding a low-rank representation of the data, and does that make learned knowledge easier to read out?

Why it matters to me: LoRA and distillation suggest much of what large models store can be re-encoded compactly. If that is general, a compact representation should be convertible into something a person can inspect.

What would change my view: Tasks where adaptation needs high-rank updates to reach full-fine-tuning quality, or where compact representations stay no more interpretable than the full model.

  • What exactly are we doing?
  • Hu et al., LoRA

Reading list archive (13 themes)

  1. Deep learning foundations

    The first AI research thread is the question behind neural networks themselves: what kinds of functions can trainable systems represent, and what architectural biases make that representation practical?

    • George Cybenko, Approximation by Superpositions of a Sigmoidal Function
    • Essay: The mental models of deep learning

  2. Architectures for representation learning

    CNNs and transformers show the central AI research move: choose a computation pattern that matches the structure of the data, then train the whole pipeline end to end.

    • Yann LeCun et al., Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition
    • Ashish Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need

  3. Efficient model adaptation

    Large models make adaptation a first-class research problem: how much can a model specialize without retraining every parameter or adding unacceptable inference cost?

    • Hu et al., LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models

  4. Controllable generation and diffusion language models

    Controllable generation asks whether generation can be steered by explicit conditions while preserving fluency, diversity, and task usefulness.

    • Li et al., Diffusion-LM Improves Controllable Text Generation

  5. Memory and test-time learning

    Frontier AI systems increasingly need mechanisms for long context, persistent memory, and adaptation during use rather than only during pretraining.

    • Google Research, Titans and MIRAS: helping AI have long-term memory

  6. Deep reinforcement learning

    Deep RL studies how trainable systems can learn useful policies from delayed, sparse, and changing feedback instead of fixed labeled datasets.

    • Mnih et al., Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning

  7. Reinforcement learning for reasoning

    Reasoning-focused RL turns model behavior into an optimization target, raising questions about rewards, emergence, distillation, and where process supervision matters.

    • DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-R1
    • DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeekMath

  8. Explainable AI as model evaluation

    Interpretability matters most when accuracy is not enough: deployment, trust, scientific discovery, fairness, and debugging all require sharper explanations.

    • Doshi-Velez and Kim, Towards A Rigorous Science of Interpretable Machine Learning
    • Essay: Peeking Inside the Black Box

  9. Feature attribution and explanation skepticism

    LIME, SHAP, saliency maps, and their critiques form a useful testbed for asking whether explanations are faithful, stable, and actually useful to users.

    • Ribeiro et al., Why Should I Trust You?
    • Adebayo et al., Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps

  10. Representation analysis and probing

    Representation analysis asks what information is encoded inside a model, how it changes across layers, and whether probes reveal structure or only probe capacity.

    • Bengio et al., Representation Learning: A Review and New Perspectives
    • Hewitt and Liang, Designing and Interpreting Probes with Control Tasks

  11. Mechanistic interpretability

    Mechanistic interpretability is the attempt to reverse-engineer neural networks as computation: circuits, features, induction heads, superposition, and scalable tooling.

    • Elhage et al., A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
    • Elhage et al., Toy Models of Superposition

  12. Agent evaluation, tool use, and verification

    Agent research should be measured by accuracy, cost, latency, repeatability, tool behavior, and whether verification loops catch errors before they compound.

    • Kapoor et al., AI Agents That Matter
    • Yao et al., ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models

  13. Routing, model fusion, and efficient specialization

    Mixture-of-experts, cascades, model merging, task arithmetic, and speculative decoding all ask how to activate only the computation a task deserves.

    • Shazeer et al., Outrageously Large Neural Networks
    • Leviathan et al., Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
